output: We had abundant food, including afternoon tea, attendants to wait on us, doctors and nurses for our health, radios, books, papers, and other recreation facilities. They even arranged frequent walks for us.

instruction: What was special about the water at the sanatorium?
output: The major-general informed us that the place was famous for its health-giving mineral springs. I didn't care for the mineral water at first, but I grew very fond of it later.

instruction: What wild hope did you harbor shortly after arriving in the Soviet Union?
output: I had the wild hope that since Britain and America were allies of the Soviet Union, I might be allowed to go and live in one of those two countries as a refugee. I even had enough jewelry with me to last me a lifetime.

instruction: How did you attempt to secure your long-term stay in the Soviet Union?
output: To ensure I could stay, I made not only verbal requests but also three written applications to the Soviet authorities over five years, asking to be allowed to stay permanently. All of them went unanswered.

instruction: How did the other 'Manchukuo' detainees' attitude differ from yours regarding their future?
output: They took a completely different attitude. Unlike me, they desperately wanted to return to China, believing their families needed them in the Northeast and that they had 'official business' to attend to.

instruction: Who were some of the other 'Manchukuo' detainees who arrived after you?
output: Chang Ching-hui, Tsang Shih-yi, and Hsi Hsia were among the others who arrived at the sanatorium a few days after me.

instruction: What did Chang Ching-hui ask you to do on behalf of the other detainees?
output: He asked me to request the Soviet authorities to let them return to China soon, explaining that their families were in the Northeast and they had 'official business' there.

instruction: What was your reaction to the other detainees' request to return to China?
output: I didn't know or care what their 'official business' might be, and frankly, I took not the slightest interest in their request. However, when they pleaded, I did pass it on to the Soviet officer in charge, but nothing came of it.

instruction: Why did the other detainees want to return to China so badly?
output: They understood the Kuomintang better than I did. They believed the Kuomintang needed them and thought they would be able to do well for themselves back home. Some of them almost went mad with longing.

instruction: How were you kept informed about the news while in the Soviet Union?
output: Soviet interpreters would tell us the news, and we often saw the Chinese-language paper, Shih Hua Pao, which was published by the Soviet Army in Lushun.

instruction: What was your stance on the Chinese Civil War?
output: I took no interest in the war. I felt it made no difference to me who won, as both the Communists and the Kuomintang, I believed, would want my life. My only hope was never to return to my country.

instruction: What were the sympathies of the former puppet ministers regarding the Chinese Civil War?
output: Their sympathies were naturally with the American-backed Kuomintang, whom they expected to win the war.

instruction: What did the former puppet ministers want to do after the defeat of the Kuomintang?
output: After the Kuomintang's defeat, they wanted to send a telegram of congratulations on the founding of the People's Republic of China, which I found quite a turnaround.

instruction: What does the phrase 'Still Giving Myself Airs' imply about your behavior in the Soviet Union?
output: It implies that despite my changed circumstances as a detainee, I continued to act with the arrogance and expectation of deference that was accustomed to from my days as emperor. I never truly shed my former imperial habits.

instruction: How did your family members address you when they couldn't use 'Your Majesty'?
output: They called me 'Above,' and continued to pay me their respects every morning, just as they had in the old days.

instruction: What personal services did your family members provide for you in Khabarovsk?
output: They would fold up my quilt, tidy the room, bring me food, and wash my clothes, essentially continuing to wait on me as they always had.

instruction: Describe the incident with the former minister at Khabarovsk.
output: One day, when I decided to go for a stroll, I saw a former minister sitting at the bottom of the staircase. When he saw me, he completely ignored my presence. I was so angry that I never thought of going downstairs again and spent my time reciting scriptures instead.

instruction: How did most of the ex-'ministers' generally treat you?
output: Most of them still behaved respectfully towards me. For example, during Chinese New Year, when we ate jiaozi, they would always give me the first bowl.

instruction: What was your attitude towards your family members working for others?
output: I was not pleased at all. I explicitly stopped my brother and brothers-in-law from laying the table for everyone else, stating that I would not have my relations waiting on anyone but myself.

instruction: What inconvenience did you face when your household members were moved to another reception center in 1947 and 1948?
output: It was most inconvenient for me, as I had never been separated from my family before. Although the Soviet authorities kindly allowed me to eat by myself, I then had the problem of who would bring me my food.

instruction: Who stepped in to help you with meals and washing during that period of separation?
output: Fortunately, my father-in-law volunteered to bring me my food and do my washing into the bargain.

instruction: What 'light labor' activity were you and your household members given?
output: We were given a small plot of land in the yard of the reception center where we could grow vegetables.

instruction: What vegetables did you attempt to grow in your plot?
output: We grew green peppers, tomatoes, aubergines, beans, and other things.

instruction: What was your experience like with gardening, and what was your primary interest in it?
output: It was a new experience for me, and I watched with fascination as the green shoots grew. I even enjoyed filling the watering can and watering them. However, my main interest was simply that I liked eating peppers and tomatoes, and I often thought it would be more convenient to just buy them from a greengrocer's.

instruction: How long did you stay in the Soviet Union?
output: I spent five years in the Soviet Union.

instruction: What was your party referred to as upon landing in Chita?
output: We were referred to as the first batch of 'Manchukuo' war criminals to arrive in the Soviet Union.

instruction: What kind of vehicle transported you from the airfield in Chita?
output: We were driven away from the airfield in a Soviet Army car.

instruction: What did the landscape look like as you drove from the airfield?
output: It appeared we were driving across a plain that stretched out black and immense on either side, then through woods, and finally climbing a narrow, bending road.

instruction: What was your initial impression of the major-general in command of the Chita garrison?
output: He announced our detention solemnly, but then told us kindly to wait calmly for a decision on our fate. He even pointed out the health-giving mineral springs.

instruction: What was the official status of civilian 'Manchukuo' officials compared to military officers?
output: The civilian 'Manchukuo' officials enjoyed the status of detainees, while the military officers were considered war criminals.

instruction: Did the Soviet authorities ever respond to your written requests to stay permanently?
output: No, all three of my written applications to stay permanently in the Soviet Union went unanswered.

instruction: What was the Soviet officer's standard reply to both your requests and those of the other detainees?
output: His standard reply was always, 'Very well, I shall pass it on,' but nothing ever came of it.

instruction: How did your feeling of 'morbid suspicion' affect you early in your detention?
output: It caused me quite unnecessary mental agony, such as when I mistook a Soviet officer of Chinese descent for a Chinese captor come to take me back.

instruction: What was your overall feeling about your life during the initial detention in the sanatorium?
output: I was quite satisfied with that life from the first, considering it a privileged detention with many comforts.

instruction: Why did you believe it would make no difference who won the Chinese Civil War?
output: My reasoning was that both the Communists and the Kuomintang, regardless of who prevailed, would inevitably want my life.

instruction: What was the atmosphere like when you first entered the large, lighted building in the mountain valley?
output: Everyone's spirits rose upon seeing it, especially after someone muttered, 'This is a hotel.' We were then greeted by a man in civilian clothes and Soviet officers.

instruction: What was your daily routine regarding meals and tea in the sanatorium?
output: We were given three large Russian meals a day, and also afternoon tea.

instruction: How did your perception of the mineral water change over time?
output: At first, I didn't care for the mineral water, but eventually, I grew very fond of it.

instruction: What significant item did you bring with you, and why?
output: I brought enough jewelry with me to last me for the rest of my life, hoping it would support me if I were allowed to live as a refugee in Britain or America.

instruction: What was the name of the Chinese-language paper published by the Soviet Army?
output: The paper was called Shih Hua Pao, and it was published in Lushun.

instruction: How did the detention conditions change when you moved to the Khabarovsk reception center?
output: While there were still people to wait on me (my family), there were no more attendants, making it slightly less luxurious than the sanatorium.

instruction: What cultural tradition did the ex-'ministers' observe with you during Chinese New Year?
output: They would always give me the first bowl of jiaozi, demonstrating their continued respect.

instruction: What was your ultimate desire regarding your return to China while in the Soviet Union?
output: My only hope was that I would never return to my country; I desperately wished to avoid it.

instruction: If you could sum up your attitude during your five years in the Soviet Union, what would it be?
output: I would say that I never stopped 'giving myself airs.' Despite my drastically altered circumstances, I maintained the mindset and expectations of an emperor, constantly seeking deference and service from those around me, even my own family.
